newsitem.title: ITALY: Bank of Italy monetary rigour draws criticism.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Italy monetary rigour draws criticism.

text.p: Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio has been covered with praise in the past for his tight monetary policy, but some analysts now believe his caution is exaggerated and might be hurting the struggling economy.
Market expectation of an interest rate cut was intense until recently, fuelled by the sharp fall in inflation which hit a 30-year low of 1.6 percent in May.

But Fazio has since made plain he is not sure inflation is beaten and has kept the official discount rate nailed at 6.75 percent since January, meaning real interest rates of five percent are much higher than in Italy's European partners.

"It is clear what Fazio's reservations are but I think it would be right to remove what I see as an excessive restriction of the monetary policy," said Riccardo Barbieri, senior economist with Morgan Stanley in London.
Lorenzo Stanca, head economist with bank Credito Italiano in Milan, agrees. "The attitude of the Bank of Italy is honestly quite puzzling," he said. "There are all the conditions for a rate cut."

Fazio wrong-footed the market at the start of the month, when he suddenly appeared to switch policy direction, turning his gaze from immediate inflation trends to a long-termer view of price and economic prospects.

"The bank is swinging from one position to another -- it doesn't have official targets other central banks have," said Giovanna Mossetti, chief economist with Milan brokers Caboto. "The objectives might be right, but the means might not be."

Some economists feel that Fazio is holding a gun to the head of Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, forcing him to introduce structural spending cuts to the welfare state and at the same time limit expected increases in indirect taxation.

"The Bank of Italy is not accountable and is caring too much about government fiscal policy which is not its concern," said one senior Italian economist, who declined to be named. "I don't know if monetary policy should be used in this way," he added.
Other analysts have also criticised the bank for its recent change in stance and believe it should be more open.
Lorenzo Codogno, chief economist at Bank of America in Milan, told Reuters Financial Television that Bank of Italy policy had been discretionary in the past and lacked transparency.
"Therefore it's not totally clear whether (Fazio) will continue to follow inflation or other targets," he added.
Certainly Fazio has exasperated the government, which is eager for lower interest charges to cut its huge debt servicing costs and has repeatedly called for a rate reduction.
"It is better for us not to ask any more or else it will never come," Prodi said in a newspaper interview on Friday.

Besides easing Italy's debt costs, the government hopes a rate cut would boost the economy, which shrank by 0.5 percent in the first quarter of 1997. Analysts agree that tight monetary policy is taking its toll, but say Fazio is looking beyond the horizon.

"Bank of Italy policy is certainly damaging the economy. However, a 50 basis point cut now would not make much difference and you might get stronger economic growth in the future because of (bank) policy," Caboto's Mossetti said.
Fazio himself believes a cut now could prove costly in the future. "Don't ask me to push the economy, it would be a very serious mistake," he told parliament earlier this month.
But some economists remain hopeful that monetary policy might still be relaxed shortly if preliminary inflation data for June due for release on Friday and Monday show low price growth.
Others analysts believe Fazio might have missed the boat.

"The bank has missed some opportunities in the past and despite the fact the discount rate is relatively at quite a high level given the state of the economy...Right now it is becoming increasingly difficult (to cut rates) because we have this tough stance from Fazio," Bank of America's Codogno said.
